The unemployment insurance commission explains as follows:
Mr- Wood, the defendant in the case, operates a real estate and tourist cabin business. Employment in that business is insurable under the Unemployment Insurance Act. The commission has experienced considerable difficulty in obtaining Mr. Wood's co-operation in the matter of making the requisite contributions to the U. I. fund, for and in respect of his employees.
Auditors of the commission have found it necessary to call on Mr. Wood several times and, on four such occasions, found him delinquent. In July, 1947 he was in default in the amount of $111.69; in August, 1948, $16.05; in August, 1949, $17.60; and in July, 1950, $5.76.
In addition to the calls made by the auditors, many letters have been written to him by the commission. Indeed, at the time of the 1949 audit he informed the auditor that he would not obtain insurance books for his employees or pay contributions in respect of an employee who was working as a carpenter. After a specific demand was made upon him to obtain books and insure the carpenter, he complied.
It is the duty of the commission to see that all contributions due to the fund are made. Default or delay in payment creates many problems, one of which is that the employees or former employees of the delinquent employer lose their rights, or part of them, when they become unemployed and seek unemployment insurance benefits. In other words, in such cases the records of the commission do not show all the entitlement of the worker; indeed, in some instances, the worker is unable to show right to any benefits because of the default of the employer. It will therefore be realized how

On (the orders of the day:

I should
like to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs or to such other member of the government as it may concern. I regret I have not given notice. Are Canadian citizens working in the United States to be subject to the United States draft law, as reported in the newspapers?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: As it happens, I have some information on that subject.
Mind reader.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I anticipated a question of this kind.
A crystal ball.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Reports appearing in this morning's press incorrectly indicate that there has been a radical change in United States policy affecting Canadian citizens who reside in Canada but work in the United States. This is not the case. Since the introduction of the selective service act all male persons residing in the United States have been liable to call-up under the United States draft law. Up to June 19 of this year an alien residing in the United States might claim exemption on the ground that he was an alien and exemption would be granted to him under forfeiture of his

right ever thereafter to become a citizen of the United States. By amendment to the selective service act on the date stated this privilege of exemption previously granted to aliens was rescinded.
The specific position with regard to Canadians living in Canada and working in the United States seems to centre about Detroit and Windsor. No person can be admitted to the United States for the purpose of engaging in paid employment in that country unless he is granted an immigration visa. It is not material to this issue where he may happen to sleep. All persons who are admitted to the United States for the purpose of engaging in paid employment are presumed to be "residing in the United States" for the purposes of the selective service act. Therefore there can be no question that under the terms of the United States selective service act Canadians who live in Windsor but work in Detroit under an immigration visa are liable to be called up under the United States selective service act in precisely the same way as United States citizens.
What was the effect of our selective service act during the war? Was it not done in consultation between the two governments?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there was consultation during the war in regard to the application in either country of selective service laws of the other. The situation is not quite the same now.
There has been no consultation with respect to this matter between the two governments?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I would have to look into that.
Since this seems to be a procedure taken unilaterally with regard to Canadian citizens, should not some representation be made to the United States government on the matter?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I doubt whether this procedure was taken unilaterally regarding Canada. I am sure it applies to all living in the United States, and not only to Canadians. I am not sure whether we have or have not made representations on the subject, but I shall be glad to look into that.
I mean unilateral action on the part of the United States with respect to Canada and not with respect to other nations.

I should like to ask the minister whether students and short-term employees cannot go to the United States unless they take out immigration papers. A number of students have taken positions in, we will
Inquiries of the Ministry say, Washington, and other places, in their university years. This has been temporary employment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Canadians I have been talking about are those who are working in the United States on immigration visas. The situation would be different in regard to * great many of our students over there.
I take it that my hon. friend from Windsor-
Essex West.

speechtext:
Thank you. I am glad you are listening.
I think it is perhaps a little odd for one who was not a member of the committee to step into this fight. Indeed, I do feel just a trifle like a camp follower. We had all the front-line troops in action yesterday, or at least some of them, and I hope we shall hear from more of them today. I hope we shall not merely have the speech of the member for Montreal St. James (Mr. Beaudry), who gave such a fine exhibition last night, but short of his vote. At any rate I am going to suggest that camp followers have their uses.
I had a recollection that the battle of Bannockburn was won by camp followers, and I have some evidence to that effect which I hope will be of interest. It is not very flattering to the English, but I hope this may be of interest to the men of Scottish descent and also, because of the ancient alliance, to those of French descent. In those days we all fought against the English. Briefly, this is a description of the outcome of the battle. The final impetus to the rout of the English was given by a historic charge of the gillies-that is the camp followers- who had been watching from the heights. They charged down the hill blowing horns, waving such weapons as they possessed and holding aloft improvised banners. Their cries of "slay", "slay", seemed to the weary English to betoken the advance of great reserves, and in a few minutes the whole English army broke and fled. I can hardly hope, Mr. Speaker, that I shall have such a dramatic effect on this assembly. At any rate, I put that forward with respect as an indication of the use a humble camp follower may have.
It is difficult to remember it perhaps, but this bill was introduced as a measure which would supposedly have some action on inflation, but that seems to have been left so far in the background now that we are dealing with it purely as it affects the Combines Investigation Act. Nevertheless, I think we should remind ourselves briefly of what was said in the speech from the throne. I quote from page 2 of Hansard lor October 9, 1951:
Every measure will be taken which my ministers believe will be effective in counteracting inflation without impairing our free institutions.
Later there is a reference to this particular measure. In spite of this fine introduction

Combines Investigation Act I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the bill has become a foundling. I understand a "foundling" is a child whose parents are unknown and cannot be discovered. While the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) sponsored the measure, through the speech from the throne, in dignified words, when he came to speak about it-I was going to say he blew hot and cold but that would not be correct because there was no hot, he really just blew cold on it. What he said was this, as recorded on page 41 of Hansard for October 15, 1951:
... as regards Immediate additional measures to curb inflation, while others may develop, the only one we are prepared to submit at this time is the one that will arise out of this report ot the combines committee with respect to resale prices.
Then he said:
I do not think that is going to have a very substantial effect on the index ot the cost of living;...
Having been rejected by the Prime Minister, the bill found itself on the doorstep of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). He seemed to have received very little help from his side of the house, except from the chairman of the committee to whose efforts I shall try to do full justice. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), whom we all remember as the guide, philosopher and friend of the Minister of Justice from two years ago when he first became famous in this house, apparently has taken no interest in this matter. We may hope that before we are finished we may have some words from him.
I want to pause for a moment to comment on the fact that the primary objective of the bill was to bring down the cost of living; and, as I say, that seems to have been lost sight of. It is getting smaller and smaller. Everyone who has spoken about that aspect of it has pooh-poohed it to the point where now we almost forget that it was ever in the picture of all. I feel it is desirable-I know the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) will be interested in this-to point out that this is the third and last of the special hopes that were held out to us in these last months for dealing with inflation. The first hope we had was economy. I am not going to take the time of the house to any greater extent than to remind you that that has gone down the drain. The parliamentary assistant, followed by the minister, has told us, not with sadness as I think they should but with the greatest equanimity, that apparently we must expect nothing from government economy. They prescribe economy for other people, but not for government.
The second great panacea or the second method of reducing prices was high taxes. We were told that they would be painful but


they would have a very salutary effect. I want to admit that at one time that was the general belief. This belief has been exploded now because we have developed elements in the community who are so strongly organized that they are able to defeat the purpose of high taxes; that is to say they are able to augment their income enough to offset the taxes. This remedy, therefore, has really passed out of existence. I was interested in observing that no less a person than the president of the Bank of Montreal referred to that in his annual address, and gave his serious opinion that we will have to revise our thinking about the effects of high taxes.
Finally we have this last remedy, and indeed it would be flattering to describe it as even a damp squib so far as inflation is concerned. The best proof of that is that no one has seriously suggested it would be effective against inflation, not even the chairman of the committee. I say, therefore, that so far as anti-inflationary effect is concerned this measure has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. We can consider this bill purely as to its validity in dealing with the question of resale price maintenance, not expecting that it is going to have any considerable effect. The Prime Minister blew cold on it early in the session, and I think it was the chairman of the committee who suggested that there was only one per cent of the products in food stores that were price controlled. At that time he was making another argument, but I think the argument can fairly be used as showing that he does not think it will have much effect in reducing prices.
As I said, I was not a member of the committee so I propose to say very little on the argument which has been made so forcefully that the committee was conducted in an unsatisfactory manner. Anyone checking the high spots of what has taken place could have no doubt but what there was backing and filling, rather as if it were a peculiar shunting yard where the trains go up and down but hardly ever get out.
First of all there was the reference to the speech from the throne, and then the doubtful opinion of the Prime Minister a day or two later. Later still came the explanation by the Minister of Justice. That is extremely interesting because, in effect, he said that they had found there is such a thing as public opinion, that public opinion had begun to assert itself, that it had made an impression upon them, and therefore they had decided that they would have a committee.
When the committee was set up, it appeared to be constituted with the end of taking a

wide view and of trying to deal with this problem on the basis of finding out the truth, even if it took some time. But there was another miscalculation and quite soon-in about a week, if I remember rightly-the committee was limited in its objective because it was found out by this time that this was a difficult matter, a matter of importance, and that really to get at the truth-which some of us feel is important-might take some little time. The operations of the committee were therefore limited and an attempt was made to take a middle course. I suggest that this course is one that would much better be called a muddled course than a middle course because I think what was done was calculated just to make the worst of both worlds.
The idea apparently was that the Mac-Quarrie report was to be taken as more or less gospel, but it was to be open to people to come along and prove-I think that was the word used by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson)-that it was wrong. I think the word "proved" was used. At any rate, that was the general intention, namely that people had to come along and knock the MacQuarrie report down.
That was, of course, something that was difficult to do because in the MacQuarrie report there were no facts; there were just opinions; and, after all, every man is entitled to his own opinion. The result of this negative method was rather odd because it really meant that, in order to save time, the committee were reduced to the position that they would in the main allow evidence only from those people who were against the report. The result of all that was that positive evidence for the views of the MacQuarrie report and for this measure we have before us was given to a strictly limited extent. Hence, when the Minister of Justice came to make his speech, the evidence he gave was scarcely, if at all, taken from the evidence of the committee but was largely the result of investigation made by his own research department. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is small wonder that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and others complained vehemently, as they are well entitled to do, against such a method of carrying on the committee.
The second reason that I find it easy to believe that the committee was conducted in an undesirable manner was the speech made yesterday by the chairman of the committee. Last Saturday the chairman of the committee was acting for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in guiding through the financial administration bill, and I thought he did a competent and orderly job. I can only wish that yesterday he had adopted the
Combines Investigation Act same tactics, because I regard this as a serious subject. I do not think this is a subject to be made the occasion for the kind of histrionic display that we had yesterday; and when I say that, I think it is the least critical thing that can be said about it. The temptation to play to the gallery was strong. I am sure that it is heady stuff-having the large majority, which we hear of so often, faithfully pounding their desks. I think I myself would enjoy it greatly.

To speak seriously, Mr. Speaker, I think we are entitled to have the chairman of a committee give a much more balanced report-and that is a conservative statement-than we had yesterday. I have noted one thing he said which I greatly regret, and I take it that that was the kind of thing that some of my colleagues here have objected to in the committee itself.

I want to read this because, first of all, it contains a sneer; and then, second, it contains a suggestion as to utterly improper conduct on the part of the business community which, so far as I know and so far as my reading of the evidence goes, was not warranted in any way by the evidence which was given. I read from the speech of the chairman yesterday as reported at page 2147 of Hansard:
If the manufacturers get together in a back room-
You see the idea, Mr. Speaker-the back room. The whole thing at once is shrouded in an atmosphere of criticism and suspicion. To my mind that is not the way in which this thing should be considered. I propose to read a report of the British committee on this subject. They had considerable difficulty. They had criticism to make of resale price maintenance, though on the whole they refused to recommend against it. But what struck me about their report was that they were trying to get at the truth. They were giving both sides. I admit that it was a report; it was not a speech in parliament;

Combines Investigation Act but I do not think that any speech in parliament by a responsible representative, least of all by a responsible person who has been head of an important committee, should descend to this kind of thing.

I will read
the quotation from the speech to which I have referred, starting again at the beginning:
If the manufacturers get together in a back room and decide that such a retail price shall be the official price, that is obviously an illegal combine and it would be up to our efficient combines branch to commence proceedings against them. If all the retailers organized together, that would also be a combine.
Because there would be more of them, it would1 be that much easier for our combines branch to find out. But if each manufacturer-
And here is the innuendo, Mr. Speaker.
-tells all his retailers at what price they are to sell, then it is easy for these manufacturers to get together informally ...
I repeat that so far as I know that was not suggested. It was left for the chairman of the committee, in his speech, to add this innuendo gratuitously. To continue:
The effect on the consumer is the same, there is artificial fixing of prices . . . That is really the case against resale price maintenance.
I cannot help wondering if that last sentence is exactly what the chairman intended to say because, if I follow his reasoning correctly, he is saying that resale price maintenance includes this horizontal meeting of manufacturers which he has insinuated is the kind of thing that took place. I put forward that interpretation. If there is any escape from it, let us have it; but that is my understanding of it. I regret that that was said. It seems to me a great pity that it should be said by anyone in this house, but most of all that it should be said by a man who had the honourable position of presiding over this important committee and who heard the evidence.
Then there is another thing that the hon. member did which I think is gravely improper. The chairman was not content to give his own opinion; he was not content to give the opinion of other members of the house-which of course he is entitled to do-but he dragged in the civil servant who was acting as clerk of that committee and quoted him.

I feel that is very, very improper. I feel that the clerk of that committee whose name was actually mentioned by the chairman has been put in a very improper and unfair position.

1 am in the
midst of making a speech, and I would like to get on with it. If the chairman of the committee finds that I have quoted him unfairly, all right, I will take it back; but that is not the way I read it. I saw his speech and that is the way I read it and I do not think I am wrong.
I suggest that this is a serious matter, Mr. Speaker, and we might try to look at it as serious men and not just toss it backwards and forwards as a political football. I hope I can do that. I am going to quote one or two views of people who are some distance removed from this assembly, and possibly thereby get a little more detachment of view.
I am going to quote first of all a man whose name is well known. While business conditions may have changed a little since the days when he was active, I do not think they have changed much. I refer to Mr. Justice Brandeis. He was a well known liberal in the United States. The word is still respectable in the United States, because it has no connotation except the true dictionary meaning. I should like to read one or two things said by Mr. Brandeis because this thing has got so involved, as I say, in party dispute and there have been so many unpleasant suggestions of improper methods that we are in great danger of forgetting what we are really talking about, and Brandeis with his clarity of expression has outlined this matter rather well. Later I wish to go on, as I said a few minutes ago, and read from the British report which shows the pros and cons, which has critical things to say, which knows the decision is a difficult one, but which eventually reaches a- decision. Brandeis, in the book called "The Brandeis Guide to the Modern World" by a man called Lief, published in 1941, at page 213 says:
I think it important that we should develop the right of producers of trademarked articles, growers as well as manufacturers, to establish by contract the price at which their products shall be sold.
And then on the same page:
The right to fix the retail selling price is not an injury but an aid to business, so far as the particular branch of business is competitive. The cry
Combines Investigation Act
against retail price fixing is based upon a misconception.
Speaking of the evils of unlimited competition-and I would just like to interject here, Mr. Speaker, for a moment, our socialist friends twit us-and this is a very easy point to make-they say: "You are in favour of competition; all right. Why are you not in favour of all competition? Why are you for and against competition?" Well, that does not bother me terribly. There is such a thing as having too much of a good thing, as we all know, and Brandeis refers to it here, that competition can sometimes produce evils. We all know that. And as far as I can make out, from whatever experience I have had, it happens very often in life. If you take a good thing and press it too far it can do you harm. If you take a whole bottle of medicine when you should take only a spoonful it can do you harm.
I read again from Brandeis what he had to say about ruthless price cutting. He says at page 215:
It is notorious that one of the methods employed by the Standard Oil Company and other trusts to create and maintain their monopolies has been to cut prices-
And so on. I shortened the quotation, but it is here for anyone to read. Then there is a further quotation which I think comes absolutely to the point; it is right on the target:
If a dealer is selling unknown goods or goods under his own name, he alone should set the price: but when a dealer has to use somebody else's name or brand in order to sell goods, then the owner of that name or brand has an interest which should be respected.
Lest I forget to say it later, it seems to me there is a great disposition here to forget the most important distinction between the overall combination in the restraint of trade, which I understand our legislation is directed against; that is to say, where I and fifty other people are manufacturing a certain article and we all get together and fix a price, and the case where I as one of the fifty manufacturers of that article want to sell my article. Now, it is open to me to open shops of my own. Nobody can quarrel with that, but if I do otherwise, if I use other shops to sell my articles, then 1 submit that at the very least any fair-minded man will say that that is entirely different from the other thing. We have certain objections to the over-all combination, and I shall read from the British report showing that they had other objections. They were forced to the conclusion that they would not recommend against it; in other words, not do what we are being asked to do now. You see, Mr. Speaker, the man who wrote that was trying to get at the truth. He

Combines Investigation Act was not trying to smear the business community. He was not putting the business community in the box and cross-examining it the way I am told it was done in this committee; and as I say, alter listening to the speech yesterday of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), if the conduct of the committee resembled in the faintest degree that speech he made yesterday, then I would say it was entirely and absolutely improperly conducted.

I want to turn to this part of the British report. Mr. Speaker, I now have yesterday's Hansard, and I think I should put on the record the exact words of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) so that there will be no doubt whatever as to the quotation that I gave. He was speaking of Mr. McGregor's evidence, and I quote from page 2152 of Hansard of December 18 as follows:
In the experience of the oldest committee clerk in this house, the oldest reporters in this house and the oldest members of parliament who heard his evidence through, they say that never had a more objective and more powerful brief been presented to a parliamentary committee.
I think that bears out fully what I said and I shall not weary the house by repeating my comments on it. I think it is a most dangerous practice and I think it is one of the things which happen, unless they are carefully on their guard, to people who retain power a long time. There is a great danger of their coming to regard themselves as demi-gods. As far as I can make out, when you come to be a demi-god a lot of things happen. There are, of course, some people who do not give way to that kind of thing.
I should like to quote from the British report because, as I say, the impression you get from that report is that they are actually trying to find out the truth. Often that seems desirable. They tried to look at both sides of the case and I shall try to quote both sides and what they said. They did not pretend that it was open and shut and they found great difficulty in reaching their conclusions. First I should like to quote from page 4 of the report of the committee on resale price maintenance of June, 1944, as follows:
19. The representatives of the various women's organizations who gave evidence before us were, without exception, strongly in favour of branding. They found it convenient when shopping not to have to examine everything they bought in order to assess its quality; they had found that the containers in which branded goods are normally sold-
I am not reading all of that. It may be that there are other things which I should read, but my time is running out and I want to
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
refer to the opposite side so that there will be no question. Another paragraph reads:
23. We have therefore assumed that manufacturers will continue increasingly to mark goods in such a way that the consumer may trace their original source. We have also assumed that, although there may be incidental disadvantages or abuses, the system by which manufacturers purposely differentiate their products from those of other manufacturers-
They do not seem to think that they are in the back room together.
-and actively promote their sale by advertisement and other means, is not, generally speaking, in conflict with the public interest.
Then on page 11 is a section headed "opposition to resale price maintenance", and I quote:
51. Fixed prices for branded articles thus prevent certain advantages to manufacturers, distributors and consumers alike, and the arguments in favour of the system which we have reproduced above are based on years of experience. They are not, however, supported by all parties and the undesirability of variations in retail price is by no means universally acknowledged.
My time is running out and I shall have to shorten these quotations. On page 15 there is another section I should like to read as follows:
70. The extent to which fixed margins will operate adversely to the public interest must in our view largely depend upon the proportion of goods to which they apply and the rigour with which they are maintained.
Then there is a reference on page 17 to loss leaders, which they consider most seriously but which I shall not attempt to deal with. I come now to the recommendations to be found on page 33. Here again there are several sections which I shall not have time to read and which point out the difficulties. Do not let it be thought that I am suggesting that these people were wholeheartedly in favour of this. I have only time to read the two operative clauses, as follows:
163. We recommend that no action should be taken which would deprive an individual producer-
That is defined as including manufacturer, wholesaler, grower, importer, etc.
-of the power to prescribe and enforce resale prices for goods bearing his name.
167. We therefore recommend that steps be taken to render illegal the application of sanctions which extend beyond the remedies open to an individual producer for any breach of resale price maintenance conditions.
As I understand it, they are against manufacturers getting together, but they approve of one man doing this. I should like to note what Mr.' Henry Smith said, and this was referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He was a member of the committee and he certainly

had great reservations because he was troubled about it. In the first paragraph of his note he said:
I support the recommendations adopted by my colleagues, as I consider that they represent a marked advance from the present position.
That is to be found on page 34. He indicates that he was troubled.

In my opinion the criticism of resale price maintenance which some of our witnesses presented, and which is set out in the report, is entirely convincing. The recommendations of our report, if adopted, will lessen these evils; but will in my opinion only remove them if it proves impossible for resale price maintenance to be operated without the support of trade associations.
All I am saying is that this man who had all those difficulties nevertheless went along with this report, and he explains why he did it. The hon. member for St. James (Mr. Beaudry) made a most interesting speech last night when he had some interesting things to say about various matters. He seemed to think that there was a great deal of make-believe. He did an adequate job and I do not propose, as I had intended to, dealing with the McGregor evidence except for one thing. I should like to point out what Mr. McGregor said when referring to loss leaders, a matter which troubled the MacQuarrie committee but which they more or less swallowed. I quote Mr. McGregor's reply at page 412 as follows:
I do not think you can put through legislation that will prevent any dealer from selling below cost.
Then on page 413 we find a qualification of that because he seems to indicate that it is possible to devise legislation. There are the two conflicting statements.
Combines Investigation Act
We have suggested that this matter be not rushed through, but that has not been treated with very great sympathy. I think there is a great deal to be said for it. In the first place, I believe that there have been many converts to this view since this discussion began. There were a great many people who thought when it began it was simply a case of saying "resale price maintenance injures competition and therefore it should be done away with,'' but I think many people have abandoned that view. I suggest to the government it should not be afraid to let public opinion run its course, and that there is no need to rush this thing. Nobody in his sane senses can suggest it is going to produce any immediate result on inflation, and I for my part can see no reason whatever to rush it through, as is apparently proposed.
One thing is clear beyond everything else, that whatever else it will do it will injure a lot of small people. I consider myself fortunate to have had the privilege of sitting in this house during this special session. I feel it has been a good session in which to be initiated into parliamentary procedure, because it has covered a tremendous amount of territory. I suppose we shall remember it as the inflation session. A great deal of the speech from the throne dealt with the problem of inflation and the high cost of living. I believe it was the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) who described this session as the "inflation session". No doubt the emphasis on that problem made it necessary for the government to seek some reasonable solution or some explanation for the difficulty that, to date, has been considered as one of the important problems in our economy.
In looking around for a solution to problems there is a well known mechanism that we adopt as individuals; we use the scapegoat mechanism. We always try to blame the other fellow. It is rare to find an individual who will stand on his own feet and say, "It is my fault". We use the scapegoat technique and we blame somebody, something or some group which is not powerful enough to fight back. I have the feeling, as I have had ever since the legislation was first introduced, that the small retail merchant is being made the scapegoat in so far as the intent of this present legislation is concerned. As I proceed with my remarks, I want to speak on behalf of the small retail merchant.
Later on in the session we moved from inflation into the deflated period, when there was hardly enough business to keep parliament occupied for a few days. I was amazed because there were important matters of business on the order paper, and as a newcomer I felt we should be digging into those as hard as we could. As a result of the "deflated period" we are now faced with the ordeal of carrying on this important debate with Christmas pressing hard upon us. It is almost unfortunate to have to disturb the serenity of the pre-Christmas period with some of the verbal displays we have seen during the last two days. It seems to me that the final phase of this session is the deflation stage. We have moved from inflation to the deflated period, and now we are in the deflation stage, because from what I can gather by reading the reports and listening to the discussions it would seem that this measure is going to


have a deflationary effect. The deflationary effect is going to be felt hardest by the small retail merchant.
I should like to read from a publication of the Canadian Association for Adult Education. On November 29 this group discussed the topic "Has big business too much power?" In dealing with the question before the house, the official pamphlet has this to say:
In 1950, In a period of high prices, the government at Ottawa set up the MacQuarrie committee to study federal combines legislation and to find out if competition were operating freely in the public interest. The committee found that it was current business practice for a manufacturer to set a "minimum resale" price for his product-that is to force the retailer to sell his product at not less than a minimum price. The committee recommended that the government pass legislation to make this sort of action on the part of the manufacturer an offence. The purpose behind such legislation, of course, would be to bring down the price of goods in some lines and thus ease the high cost of living.
We have bad that point answered by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). Continuing to quote from the article, I read:
Here we have an interesting situation. It is the big retail firms in Canada which stand to benefit from such action. As a matter of fact, one of our largest department stores has been a leader in urging the government to carry out the recommendation of the MacQuarrie committee.
It is the corner store retailer, in the main, who would like to see the manufacturer go on holding the price line on his product. The small retailer welcomes the protection of "minimum resale" prices, or "fair trade" prices, as they are called, because they mean he can retain his margin of profit, and still give "service" to his customers. No one can undersell him past a point because the retail price of the product is not allowed to go below a definite figure. In this case, then it would seem that what the MacQuarrie committee thinks to be in the public interest fairly well coincides with the position of the big retailer.
That was an objective appraisal of the possible consequences of this legislation now before the house.
The legislation has had a rather devious course. That is quite evident. It was introduced early in the session and then sent back to a committee for discussion. Then the committee was cut off abruptly before the retail merchants association had a chance to give evidence. The Ottawa Citizen of November 2 had something to say on this rather unusual procedure:

I submit that the enforcement of it will be as difficult as the enforcement of the prohibition against the consumption of alcoholic beverages, now an unhappy memory. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because of the ramifications of the retail trade and, as a matter of fact, of the entire business of manufacturing, jobbing, wholesaling and retailing, to say nothing of the small drug stores, grocery stores, haberdashers and other small retailers. I hope to show later in my remarks that the enactment of this measure will dislocate the normal course of business in this country. I say that one of my reasons for opposing it is the fact that it is another prohibition. It will, in fact, create a species of grey markets, or if not grey markets at least grey agreements. It will be most difficult to completely police this measure.
On the very simple question of a manufacturer withholding goods from a retail outlet that has cut prices, it will be found that prosecution is extremely complex and evidence extraordinarily difficult to obtain. If there is a concentrated drive against this legislation by the small retailers, as there may well be, the policing of the measure may require a great number of people in the combines administration. As I have said, this legislation is obviously unpopular with a great number. Difficulty will be experienced in registering convictions through the ordinary process of a jury trial. I point that out as being one of the disadvantages of the enactment of this legislation, especially when there is obviously a great body of opinion opposed to it.
I also oppose this legislation, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it is unconstitutional. It restricts the freedom of contract which is a civil right, and restricts it in such a way that even fair and reasonable contracts are prohibited. Not being learned in the law I do not put myself up as a professional witness in this regard, but it seems to me that the freedom of contract is a basic and inalienable right under the British North America Act. If it does anything this legislation restrains the freedom of contract. This may in the government's opinion be desirable, but I do

What is the logical and almost immediate result of this legislation? It is going to concentrate an even greater volume of business in the main shopping centres. I happen to have some knowledge of the conditions in the city of Toronto, particularly concerning the main shopping artery, downtown Yonge street. I am informed by people whose duty it is to inform me that if this legislation goes through there will be an even greater flow of business from the small retail merchants to this main shopping artery. These are not. small stores on Yonge street. Property on that street has a value of many, many thousands of dollars per foot, so they must be big businesses. The information given to me by people whose duty it is to give it to me is that there will be a greater concentration of business in this area. I want to go on to the recent result-and I think it is germane to this discussion-of price wars in the United States. There is here an example which I think we can regard as a reasonable sample of what we may expect. In the city of New York there was a violent price war put on by Gimbel's, Macy's and one or two of the other large department stores. Apart from the subsequent legal question of certain manufacturers suing the stores for selling their goods below the agreed-on price, the result has been that prices today, of the goods which were subject to that price war, and which were most intensively used as loss leaders, are now back again and judging by last week's New York press, are actually selling at a higher price than that at which they sold before the price war took place.
There price wars were, of course, conducted on a cash basis, and extremely drastic reductions took place for a short time. But the people they benefited', if they benefited anybody, were the comparatively minuscule group who happened to be at that moment in the market for the particular items which were subject to drastic price cutting. Those and those only benefited from the price war.
Mr. Speaker, I believe it would be interesting for the house to hear what the late

Mr. Justice Louis D. Brandeis has to say on this subject, from the legal point of view. He said:
Already the displacement of the small independent businessman . . . presents a grave danger to our democracy. The social loss is great; and there is no economic gain . . . Shall we, under the guise of protecting competition, further foster monopoly by creating immunity for the price-cutters?
America should be under no illusions as to the value or effect of price-cutting. It has been a most potent weapon of monopoly-a means of killing the small rival to which the giant trusts have resorted most frequently. It is so simple, so effective. Farseeing organized capital secures by this means the co-operation of the short-sighted unorganized consumer to his own undoing. Thoughtless or weak, he yields to the temptation of trifling immediate gain and, selling his birthright for a mess of pottage, becomes himself an instrument of monopoly.

I now come to the general question of inflation, Mr. Speaker. This legislation has been introduced in the belief, or on the supposition, that it is anti-inflationary, despite the fact that the Prime Minister stated that it would have very little effect, despite the fact, as has been shown over and over again in this debate, that the amount of goods purchased through price maintenance is a small percentage of the average weekly budget, or the factors which go into the dominion bureau of statistics cost of living index. Despite that fact, as has been shown over and over again, the reason for this legislation keeps on being given as an anti-inflationary measure.
Let us show very simply what is inflation, Mr. Speaker. Inflation is now, has been in the past and always will be, caused by an increase in the supply of money, not equalled by an increase in the supply of goods. Nothing has altered that since the time of Diocletian, and this measure is in many ways similar to parts of the edict of Diocletian and parts of the Sumerian code, and parts of the laws put down at the time of the great inflation in France, and it will have basically the same economic effect; the only

difference being that in the time of Robespierre the French government had the use of the tumbril and the guillotine. These economic prohibitions have always brought disaster to those who tried them. Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, on the broad question whether this will aid in curbing inflation, by admission and by evidence already brought out in this debate the answer must be no.
Coming now to my own particular constituency of York West, I received a very great number of letters and telegrams; and during the time of the Ontario election, and afterwards, I made it my business to visit as large a number of my constituents as possible who had either written to me, sent me telegrams or in other ways communicated with me. In only one case did I find that the communication had been inspired or suggested by others. In the other cases-and I have some 65 telegrams in front of me-the actions were based on a genuine fear which the small druggist and the small retail merchant have as to what would happen to them should this legislation pass. I cannot neglect that body of opinion. I cannot believe that that body of opinion, expressed freely and without prompting or without coercion in any way, represents anything but a genuine fear and a true and honest opinion of the small retailer and the small merchant in my riding. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, having regard to this evidence, even if I wanted to, I could not possibly support this piece of legislation, based on the simple equation of the greatest good for the greatest number. There can be no question that these small retailers, the small druggists, the little general merchants and the specialty shops in a growing suburban district, are definitely afraid of what will happen should the trade that they are slowly building up in a new district be siphoned off by means of the loss leader to the main downtown stores.
Again, Mr. Speaker, there is no evidence, there is no suggestion that any action will be taken to cope with the loss leader device in this legislation. I submit, again on the evidence given in the price wars in New York, that the loss leader, to be effective, must maintain a reduction of probably 30 per cent to 35 per cent. Take a brand name product, cut it 35 per cent, 40 per cent or even 50 per cent and you create a magnet that will draw the people from the districts of any community to the central shopping section. You cannot help it. I know this because stores in the central part of Toronto have intimated it. It has proved to be so in New York. Even with transportation difficulties as they are, the opportunity of saving a large percentage will certainly attract the buyers.

Mr. Speaker, I
am pleased to take part in this debate. First of all, I congratulate the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the members of the cabinet for having introduced a bill which will be passed, I hope, by a large majority.
I am speaking today on behalf of the electors of Russell and also as a small general merchant, as a small retailer with thirty-five years of experience, seven as manager of

a store and twenty-eight as owner. I say, and truly so, that I am a general merchant since we sell drugs, groceries, hardware, dry goods, all kinds of building materials, feed, farm implements, trucks, tractors and jewelry, rings and watches. In other words we sell everything from pins to a truck, a tractor or bulldozer, goods worth from five cents to $25,000.
I can therefore claim a fair amount of familiarity with the retailer's problems. I must say that the position taken by our friends of the opposition does not surprise me in the least, because I have been following their policy for over twenty-five years. They have not changed. In fact I believe they are getting less and less serious; we all remember that they repeatedly stated, between 1945 and 1949, that we should do away with all controls. At that time, the Liberal government deemed it wise to remove controls gradually as the supply became sufficient to meet the consumers' demand. Yet since 1949, that same group has been asking the government to reimpose controls which they have themselves condemned.
During the last session, we have been criticized for doing nothing to check inflation. When legislation was introduced to curb the extravagant amount of credit granted on items, most of which were not essential to the population's well-being, this helpful legislation was again criticized, although it had greatly reduced the price of certain goods, especially automobiles, refrigerators as well as a large quantity of other goods. I think I know something about this since, in my store, I have a pretty complete line of goods for sale. I never fail to advise people not to go too deeply into debt because, as everyone knows, it is always the less well off that suffer most since their creditors force them to pay up, even though they might thereby lose all they have.
Right now we listen to the Conservatives upholding price maintenance in the name of the small retailer. Come, my friends, let us be more serious about this! You wish to protect the financier, the manufacturer, the wholesaler, the chain store operator. More than that, you want to turn one small group into the dictators of Canadian trade and make the small retailers their slaves. Should you succeed we would merely be the distributors for that group which would henceforth bend us to their will. Again the little people would be duped. In this way combines and trusts would grow more numerous and powerful and the retail trade of this

country, in the very near future, would be controlled and directed by a few hundred individuals.
No, Mr. Speaker. I submit that the small retailer like myself, whether he is a general merchant or a grocer, is one of those who have done very great service to Canada. The small shopkeeper is his customer's friend. Always ready to serve him honestly, he lives with him and is at all times prepared to be of service. He helps his community in all its social assistance activities, does his very utmost to improve his town or city and works in the interests of both workers and farmers. His outlook being such, he therefore does not want to be compelled to make a higher profit than he thinks is fitting; he is capable of obeying the laws of the land but he is opposed to the dictatorship of certain sections of society.
Mr. Speaker, retail price maintenance is harmful to 95 per cent of the people of Canada, even to a great many of those who are in favour of it. It allows too large profits to be made. People are much more intelligent than our Conservative friends seem to think.
When the margin of profit is too wide, the buyer realizes it and cuts down his purchases. The manufacturer is unable to sell his goods: that is against the interests of the industrialists themselves since it leads to unemployment. The people who, due to circumstances, are compelled to buy those goods pay too much; they are taken advantage of and that leads to a rise in the cost of living.
The small merchant who is compelled to sell certain goods at fixed prices does not dare reduce his prices for fear of not being permitted to buy other supplies. On the other hand the large stores, due to their purchasing power, are much more independent; if the manufacturer refuses to sell them his products he risks losing a large customer and he knows quite well that this large store can buy elsewhere. Furthermore, the large retailers advertise much through the medium of catalogues, radio, newspapers, etc. They advertise other goods which draw the customers and are thus able to sell their wares at fixed prices. Customers are allowed discounts on certain goods when purchasing such and such an article sold at a set price. Most often these are items the customer could easily do without for the time being.

No, Mr. Speaker, the small retailer is not asking for any favours. All he wants is to be treated the same as others; he wants to do business unfettered. Why should the manufacturer treat him so unfairly. Why should he grant the large store discounts of 10, 15 and even 25 per cent more than is given the small retailer?
I would not mind an additional 2 to 5 per cent discount, since it does cost a little less to sell and deliver in large quantities, but there should never be more than a 5 per cent difference between the small retailer and the large retailer. From the information made available to us it is clear that the small retailer sells the greater part of the manufacturer's production and it is through him that both manufacturers and wholesalers make their profits.
The small retailer should be the one to be assured of reasonable protection on the part of manufacturers. If the latter continue to protect more and more chain stores of every description, department stores and all types of establishments with great purchasing power, they will soon find themselves at the mercy of the operators of these stores who will dictate to them the price which they are willing to pay, will make them produce at a loss, thus forcing them to cut their employees' salaries or close shop altogether. These large retailers will then have their own way with the manufacturers, the small retailers and the consumers of this country. They will thus tell us what to do, while continuing to exploit us.
I leave to our friends, the Tories, the task of defending their friends, these few millionaires who think only of increasing their profits but forget that Canadians are not so easily deceived.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I ask my government to continue, as in the past, to protect the interests of the less privileged people, who cannot defend themselves as well as others. I take this opportunity of inviting all Canadians to make a still greater effort to increase production of essential commodities, not only to meet the needs of every Canadian but also to enable us to help the people of less fortunate countries than our beautiful Canada. We will thus help fight inflation and assist people of countries less privileged than ours. This would draw upon us the gifts of divine Providence, permit us to check communism and contribute to increase the respect of other peoples for Canadians.
In conclusion, I say that we will not only prove that we have a dignified and great

Combines Investigation Act Prime Minister, but that the whole Canadian people is following his example, and wants to see Canada prosperous, while helping to Ensure .prosperity in other countries.

Mr. Speaker, in this debate I have seen a number of lawyers and others metaphorically donning their gowns and getting in behind the counters. Because prior to coming here I had 25 years of business experience, I should like to give the house some of my impressions, gathered out of that experience, as to the effectiveness of this legislation. I was in a business where we acted as manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, a rather unique position. We endeavoured to establish our retail prices by quite extensive advertising. We found that some retailers we supplied broke our retail prices. In all the years I was irx business we did not do a single thing by way of reprisal against any of those people because in my mind-although I did not know it; I never inquired-I would have thought that it was against the law. I think we would be much safer in this country if we always have regard to this fact, that when a seller disposes of an article to a buyer the seller has severed his connection with that article; and when a person owns an article he has a perfect right to do with it as he sees fit.
I am supporting this legislation not because I think it is going to have any large-scale effect on the cost of living. I do not think it will roll back our inflationary trends very far, but I am supporting it because I think that security and not initiative has become the first consideration of too many business firms in this country for their own good. There has been a portrayal on the other side of the house that this is going to result in harsh and bitter times for retailers. I do not believe they can produce any evidence to that effect at all. I will tell you what I think it will do. Because I believe there are going to be cut prices in some lines, I think it is going to result in the greatest stimulation of sales in this country in the last year. That is what I jhink will happen.
Our state of business is not determined by .egislation such as is involved in this bill. The state of business is determined by the fantastic ability of a public when aroused to do without. That is how it is arranged. So-called good times in business occur when a man says to himself: "I must buy this article today because I think it will cost more tomorrow." Recessions in business occur when a man says: "I will put off buying this today because

I think it will be cheaper tomorrow". Buying patterns are the result of a great measure of mass psychology in people. You get great masses of people who say: "We had better wait a while and we will buy more cheaply." Those are the things that affect business and always will affect business.
One of the recent phenomena in business is the growth of business associations. I do not like to speak about conventions, because a great many of the conventions that are held today are the veritable parliaments of the industries concerned and they do a very great deal of good to industry; but almost everybody today is having a convention, and some of them in the most peculiar places, the farther away the better. I know where they grew up. They grew up in the good times we have had in the last ten years in this country, and many of them have developed because the instigators knew that first Ilsley and now Abbott would be paying for them. I feel there is this feeling on the part of some of those who are heading these conventions, that we are going to be able to be more secure in our business with possibly less effort than we have had in the past. In the old days you used to say that of every one hundred businesses that were formed, seventy-five were going to be out of business in five years. That is a thing which the businessman today is trying to avoid. He does not want to take any more risks than he has to.
There is a great demand in this country for individual security, and it is natural today. I think there is an attempt in the country to obtain business security and the security of corporations. I have this idea, that were that to be guaranteed by any means it would probably mean the denial of security to the individual. I believe that a number of the consequences and results that have flowed from any industrial associations constitute a most disquieting and indeed dangerous phenomenon in our recent industrial development. I am not going to say that the work of all industrial associations is wrong. I think the exchange of credit information, for instance, results in a social good so long as a blacklist is not compiled out of that exchange.
I have seen-and I must say I saw some evidence of it in the committee that sat here-the development of what I term a new aristocracy of business, and I do not think it is either a sound or a good thing. The businessman today,. in his relations with his government, apparently does not want to come down to see government. He has intercessors here. They are a group of high-priced legal help, groups of high-priced accountants and professional advocates of special causes,

and a number of them were before that committee. At the best they had nothing more than a superficial knowledge of what they were talking about. The best advocate for business I saw there was the old gentleman Hougham, who is now retired in the province of British Columbia, a man with a great deal of experience of his own in business. He was accorded by the group that brought him there some ten minutes, I think, but their lawyer who said he had intensively studied this subject for two weeks spent a day before the committee. Well, I think that business will do itself a great deal more credit if in its relations with government it sends practising businessmen to see governments instead of professional help such as these. I seem to read that there is some attempt here to assure profit without risk, without too much conflict and indeed without too much effort. That has not been the history of business on this continent. I think it is socially unsound for business to attempt to ensure profits upon that basis. I believe it has to be prepared to take risks, because it has built itself on that basis. Indeed, this continent has built itself on that basis. My friends of the C.C.F. opposite will not agree with me, as they do not think there is such a thing as free markets any more. I realize that today free markets are compromised by the situation that exists throughout the world, but .the closer we keep to free markets the more secure we will be. I am quite certain it will be a better day for business if business returns to the free competitive market.

Even if any member was predisposed to support in general principle the idea of making it illegal to enter into any arrangement in regard to the retail prices of goods of various kinds, I suggest that a sense of responsibility to the supreme authority of this House of Commons, this high court of parliament, would indicate to him that we should not take action of this kind, having such sweeping consequences, when we have had so little evidence, I might say no real evidence, before us upon which to act.
Others describe this as the high court of parliament. We are members of that high court of parliament. As members of that high court of parliament we have a duty to maintain its dignity and its traditions. We have a duty to maintain public respect for the procedure by which the laws of this country are enacted. No matter what emotional approach there may be to a subject of this kind; no matter what inclination there may be to simplify the manner in which we shall deal with this extremely important question of inflation, no member of this house should be prepared to cast his vote in support of something which will have a tremendous effect upon the whole established commercial structure of Canada without being able to say: I have heard the evidence and on that evidence I am convinced that this is what we should do. To hear some of the arguments that have been made-arguments, I repeat, unsupported by evidence-one would think that the passing of this bill into law is something of immense importance to the consumer. Yet within the past few minutes we have heard an hon. member, who referred to his long business experience and who said that he proposes to support the measure, tell us nevertheless that he is not supporting it because he thinks it will have much effect in reducing prices or lowering the cost of living but, if I understand what he said, in the belief that completely free competition is a better economic process than some measure of restraint such as has become established in the country over the years.
That is an understandable argument, but I would point out it is one that relates entirely to economics and trading practices, and that not one word the hon. member spoke suggested that in his mind there was anything in the nature of a criminal offence in trade arrangements of this kind. When the hon. member expressed his opinion as a businessman that the measure was not going to have any substantial effect on prices he was repeating exactly what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said earlier in this session. If we accept the opinion of the Prime Minister, if we accept the opinion of the hon. member

who has just spoken and who bases his opinion upon his years of business training, then we are not discussing something which is going to have much effect in stemming the tide of inflation. Yet it was in that light that this measure was placed before us.

Yet by his own statement, and from statements made by other members who support him, it is not anticipated that it is going to effect any substantial reduction in prices.
After all, there is statistical support for that view. One of the businesses which would be most affected by the complete abolition of agreements as to prices for various articles would be the drug business. That has been quite frankly admitted. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and others have recognized it. Therefore it seems to me that certain figures should be before the house to indicate what has been happening in the drug business compared with other retail marketing, to show just how serious this is. The last figures available as to the increase in items sold in drug stores compared with the period of 1935-39, which is used as the base period for the cost of living index, are the figures for January 15, 1951. It may be that the bureau of statistics has later figures, and if so I would be very pleased if they were placed before the house, but these are the last figures I have been able to obtain.
They show that in relation to the base period of 1935-39 some 319 drug store items, taken as representing the broad basis of this business, had risen to 122-2 compared with the figure of 100 for the base period I have mentioned. The nearest figure I have as to the cost of living index is that for February 1, 1951, and that was 175-2 compared with the figure of 100 for the same base figure of 1935-39. Thus we see that while the cost of living index had risen by 75-2 points up to that time from the base period, the increase in the cost of 319 representative items sold in drug stores was 22-2 points.

But, to answer still further the question of how this can be done, I would say that the place the government can best tackle this problem is in its taxation. This bill is not put before the house with any thought that it is going to reduce the cost of living substantially, or that it is going to halt inflation. If the government had any idea of trying to reduce the cost of living at this time it would have brought before the house a budget of some kind which would have made it possible to remove that 25 per cent increase in the sales tax that was unnecessarily introduced this spring, a tax which is directly inflationary in all its applications. It would also have removed those special excise taxes it introduced, and would have removed some of the credit restrictions it put into effect this spring-not all of them, but some of the severe credit restrictions that have had such a serious effect upon building, and upon housing, and upon other matters that are directly related to the comfort and housing of our people.
When I say that, let me point out that some measure of restraint on credit was highly desirable, and to the extent that it was desirable we would certainly commend it. But in case we have any of those very lightly-made remarks about the fact that we suggest something, and then say why it should not have been done, may I point out that the government itself has made it quite clear that it believes there is some maximum point beyond which taxation or restrictions cannot go without defeating its own purpose. That was the very argument made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he introduced the budget last spring. At the time it was suggested that an additional tax be imposed on some articles that are already heavily taxed, he said that while it had been agreed that it was a good thing to tax those particular articles, there was a point beyond which you could not go.
What has happened since that time has amply demonstrated at least the correctness of the general observation made by the Minister of Finance at that time. We have seen in the case of cigarettes that there is certainly a point beyond which you cannot go in,

Combines Investigation Act on the one hand, collecting taxes and, on the other, continuing to have the respect of the public for the laws of the land. We have had arguments in the house which have suggested that this does not meet with the entire disapproval of every member in the house. But, quite apart from that situation, the government could have taken anti-inflationary steps and could have tackled effectively the problem of the cost of living, if it had removed that 25 per cent increase in the sales tax, and removed some of the unnecessary excise taxes on things which most people find it necessary to buy.

In the very nature of things goods that have been on sale at Christmas, and which are carried over, are not kept on the shelves. Perhaps the Financial Post had some reason for believing that this was correct. What reason is there? Why could not the joint committee have sat through in the ordinary way? Why should we not at this time be passing a resolution empowering that committee to continue sitting between sessions to hear evidence? It did not complete the hearing of evidence, and no one will seriously suggest that it did. Why are we being asked to rush this legislation through? First of all, because this is the only measure the government has offered to the public in answer to its demand that something be done about the cost of living. Moreover the government is well aware that, if further evidence were heard, a great deal would be put before the committee to raise a question as to whether or not this is the wisest course.

Reference has been made to an editorial in the Kingston Whig-Standard. I propose to put part of it on the record, because although some members may have received a copy of it, possibly all have not read it. I also am not forgetful of the fact that there are those outside of the house who read Hansard, and who may be interested in an analysis of this situation which in no way reflects upon any member of the house. It does indicate the opinion of a newspaper, in this case published by a prominent and highly respected Liberal who lives in Kingston. I shall quote the last two paragraphs of that editorial of December 12, 1951:
It is significant, we think, that only one group so far, if we may judge from the evidence submitted to date to the parliamentary committee, is wholeheartedly in favour of outright abolition of resale price fixing. That group is composed of a number of mass buyers and sellers of merchandise- firms which may be described as the giants in Canadian merchandising. Their approval of abolition strongly suggests that the fears of the small merchandisers are well founded, and that the latter would be at least severely and unfairly handicapped by legislation which would permit huge rivals to sell at a fractional profit or even at a loss. Since the practice of using "loss leaders" or sharply cut prices to swell the number of visitors to stores is by no means uncommon, the position of the small merchant becomes apparent.
The entire question of resale price fixing is definitely not a simple one, as we noted above. It is complex, and its very complexity should be sufficient to indicate that a simple solution like abolition will not solve the problem. For our part, we think the government could very well forget about resale price fixing for the moment, and concentrate upon the strengthening and rigid enforcement of the laws forbidding price-fixing by combines. If these are effective in assuring unrestricted competition, there would seem to be very little to be feared from resale price fixing as it is now practised.
Although I am reminded that this editorial has been sent to many of the members, it was quite evident to me that they had not all read it. In fact I find some of them reading it even at this moment.

Of course this is not in any way as simple as it seems. I think in this case the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will recall the very substantial change that had taken place at a later date in regard to this act which was introduced, as has been pointed out, by the Liberal government and which remained substantially in that form until some years later.
Those reports that have been referred to by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) were not commissioner's reports; they were not reports similar to the one to which he referred when he spoke about this matter as being slightly delayed. It is important to remember the great difference which has taken place in the act as it indicates the evolution that has occurred and why we regard it as being so important that there should be a general review at this time of the Combines Investigation Act to bring the evolution further still more in keeping with our changing commercial and trading practices in this country.
The act at the time the hon. member mentions called for an entirely different procedure. I might say that it was not 1925, as the hon. member stated, but 1923 when it was introduced. That act placed certain responsibilities upon the registrar, who was a permanent official and who was Mr. McGregor at the time. The procedure followed at the time the five reports he has mentioned were prepared was that the registrar would make a preliminary investigation. He then reported to the minister who examined the report. The report was made to the minister simply for the purpose of consideration. If it was regarded by the minister as justifying that course, the minister would appoint a commissioner or commissioners to conduct an investigation. When the commissioner or commissioners had made their report, then and then only would the provisions of section 28 of the act as it was apply as to publication. That provision was quite similar to the provision which has been carried forward and which applies at this time to the reports of the commissioner under the act.


The five reports that were tabled were not reports that called for publication. That was the act introduced in 1923.
