This government does a great
many things of which we entirely disapprove. So far as that is concerned, may I suggest that there may have been excellent reasons for not publishing the reports when publication was not demanded. We believe, and I think most members of the government believe, that business should have some chance to be heard and be given an opportunity to state its case. The mecnanism that is now provided approaches this problem with some idea of giving the business people of this country, as well as others, an opportunity to state their case.
Let us dispose of any suggestion that those other reports were withheld under circumstances in any way similar to those under which the flour milling combines report was withheld. I think the best statement to be found on this subject is contained in the memorandum of resignation of Mr. McGregor, presented to the minister to whom he was

responsible on October 29, 1949. The minister will remember that memorandum because there was a great deal of discussion about it. In fact that memorandum had a good deal to do with smoking out that report. I should like to read the first three paragraphs and part of the fourth of that memorandum of resignation of Mr. McGregor, dated October 29, 1949, as follows:
The principal circumstances which have led me to submit my resignation as commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act can be stated briefly.
First and foremost is my deep concern about certain tendencies that have been apparent in recent months which in my opinion seriously threaten the usefulness of this legislation.
One of the principal remedial measures provided by the Combines Investigation Act is the publication of reports of investigations.
May I emphasize the words that follow:
The withholding for so many months of publication of a report which the act requires shall be made public as soon as possible after its receipt (this is the only instance of the kind in my experience) is one illustration of the tendencies I have in mind.
Closely related to this are the differences of opinion on basic policy that have been revealed in our recent discussions relating to the flour investigation and report.
I am not raising any question of your obvious right and the right of anyone to point out errors in any work I have done. The criticisms made, however, have not been directed particularly to any error of fact in my report but primarily to the policy that was followed. You have expressed the opinion that the inquiry should never have been started.
There is the reason Mr. McGregor resigned; that for the first time in his experience-he had been registrar long before the earlier date mentioned by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano until he became commissioner- there had been a withholding of a report of that kind.
I have mentioned this simply to clear the record which was placed before us yesterday. But, Mr. Speaker, I have also mentioned it for another reason. When we are told that this committee seriously attempted to examine this subject and that it was objective in its approach to this problem, then I would only add that anyone who makes that statement should read the speech made in the house yesterday by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair), a cheap, tawdry political speech by the member who had been chairman of the committee. Instead of coming here having in mind the responsibility he was called upon to accept as chairman of the committee, he came here and made a tubthumping political speech which doubtless relieved his own feelings and appeared to bring a certain measure of satisfaction to members on the other side who are not too happy about this legislation anyway. But it was not a contribution in keeping with the
Combines Investigation Act consideration deserved by legislation that is going to affect, whether for good or for bad, thousands and thousands of small merchants across the country and those who deal with them.
Again may I say that the speech made last night by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix) was another which suggested that perhaps the Financial Post was not so far wrong when it offered its explanation as to why this legislation was held back so long and then, having been held back so long, is now to be put through with such indecent haste. The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency in his remarks last night was echoing those meaningless and very worn-out propaganda arguments that this was an example of the subservience of the Conservative party to big business. What a preposterous argument when you examine the measure we are considering and the circumstances that surround its presentation to the house.
As was pointed out in earlier speeches and in editorials in papers not unfriendly by any manner of means to this government, the only people who appeared to be anxious to have this legislation passed, so far as the committee was concerned at any rate, were those very big businesses which apparently would stand to gain by the abandonment of these long established practices. I am not going to engage in any exchange of pleasantries about big business or little business. I do say that the little businesses that are close to the people right across this country are the backbone of the commercial life of Canada, but I also say that as Canadians we should not condemn any business simply because of its size. I most earnestly suggest that we recognize that these big businesses have also advanced our commercial practices.
The fact is that we want businesses big and small competing fairly and properly and in the general interest of the public under laws that are in the best interests of the people of Canada. But if there is to be any division on the basis of big business and little business, then most certainly on this occasion the government has aligned itself with big business; and it comes with very bad grace for the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency to pull out these rusty darts and throw them around as loosely as he did last night without any regard to what the real target is and what it is we are really trying to do. If there is any alignment with big business look across the aisle from me now and see where that association lies. Big business? Why, I interpolated a remark last night when the hon.

Combines Investigation Act member for Quebec-Montmorency was speaking in such unflattering terms and using phrases that might very well have been questioned if we had seen fit to do so, and asked if the speech which was being read had been prepared by one of the other hon. members; because I recognize that when it comes to big business there are experts on the government side who are able to speak about this very practice from their own knowledge over many years. I thought perhaps he had been seeking some expert advice and conceivably even had had a few choice phrases prepared which were the product of that long experience in this very activity.
We certainly are considering something that affects every Canadian today; and the consideration with which one should start every approach to this problem is the public interest. Is it in the public interest or is it not? If it is in the public interest then it should be supported. If it is not in the public interest then most certainly steps should be taken to deal with that subject. There is nothing incorrect on the record. What I have done is to use 319 representative items. And I suggest that if the minister was properly accepting his responsibility as the minister supporting this measure, and asking us to pass upon it, he should have given us some information which really showed that this was a matter, in this particular type of business, which should be dealt with by legislation of this kind.
Now, so far as this measure is concerned, there is one particular consideration which I have already suggested should always be in our minds. I refer to the public interest. The minister is well aware that in the Combines Investigation Act itself there is an attempt to measure any offence in connection with combines upon the basis of public interest. As he knows, where an offence is created in relation to a combine, there is a reservation in that respect. In that part of the act which defines a combine it makes reference to certain specific things such as:
(a)	limiting facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing, or
(b)	preventing, limiting or lessening manufacture or production, or
(c)	fixing a common price or a resale price, or a common rental, or a common cost of storage or transportation, or
(d)	enchancing the price, rental or cost of article, rental, storage or transportation, or
(e>
preventing or lessening competition in, or substantially controlling within any particular area or district or generally, production, manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, storage, transportation, insurance or supply, or
(f) otherwise restraining or injuring trade or commerce,
All this comes under the word "combine". And then the section continues:
-or a merger, trust or monopoly, which combination, merger, trust or monopoly has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public, whether consumers, producers or others.
Combines Investigation Act
The interesting words there are "which . . . has operated or is likely to operate to the detriment or against the interest of the public".
Then we come to the Criminal Code, and we find there is a reservation, in somewhat similar language, where it says that it is an offence to "unduly prevent or lessen competition". And that word "unduly" means, and has been interpreted to mean, to an extent that is not reasonable in relation to the public interest. So the consideration has been the public interest. In all these matters that is the thing that has always been borne in mind.
In this particular case there is no such reservation. There is an absolute and complete banning of a system that has grown up over many years and which, with constant extensions, has been operating I should think during the lifetime of everyone in the house, at least to some extent. We all recognize that the practice has been increasing in recent years and has become so deeply embedded in our whole commercial system that, to say the least, we would be doing something that would have very far-reaching effects if we were to pass a measure having such wide powers as the measure before us.
The interesting thing is that in all the arguments put forward there has been an assumption, without any supporting evidence -and I repeat "without any supporting evidence"-that there are sound reasons why this practice should be abandoned. There has been no attempt to analyse and dispose of the arguments put forward as to why this practice should be continued.
One of the things, of course, which has been put forward, and which was mentioned by the minister in his remarks, was the fear that has been expressed by the small businessmen across this country who have been, to some extent at least, following this practice, that this would create a further centralization of commercial power in the hands of monopolies. One of the instruments they fear, and one of the devices to which they have referred in their arguments, is that which is known as the loss leader. The minister quoted a definition of a loss leader which had been given, and which I agree does not adequately define the loss leader, as he correctly pointed out. For the reason that we have not had before us an adequate definition of a loss leader, I want to put on the record what I believe is as clear a statement as to what a loss leader really is as I have yet seen. I wish to quote

Combines Investigation Act briefly from an article in the December edition of Cosmopolitan magazine under the heading "When is a bargain not a bargain?":
Not so long ago a retailer advertised dollar bills for sale at ninety-five cents. Nice, crisp greenbacks fresfi from the United States mint. Only one to a customer. No deliveries. No exchanges. No telephone orders. People flocked to the store. You might have been in the crowd yourself, because you certainly can recognize a bargain when you see one. You might also have wondered how dollar bills could be sold for ninety-five cents. Your good sense told you that fools go broke and that philanthropists practise charity strictly after business hours.
That being the case, was there a catch in this curious sale? There was, of course. A very simple catch, as old as this country, but modernized and streamlined for superefficient hoodwinking.
The retailer knew that people would be attracted to his store. He knew that most customers would also buy a lot of the merchandise displayed on counters and shelves. In the prices of these goods were hidden the retailer's handsome profits.
The dollar bill sale, although it happened only once, symbolizes and dramatizes the extremes to which these come-ons go. Retailers offer something -called a "loss leader"-for nothing. They build their bait around national brand products whose value is as familiar to you as the worth of a dollar bill. They advertise these selected, honourable products at a cut price. Then competitors meet that price or slash below it so that they, too, can be regarded by the public as sterling champions of the consumer.
The price cutting on these products goes on and on until it may become possible to buy merchandise at less than the cost of its container. Dazzled by the bargain, very few customers realize that the retailer is no more cutting prices than the magician on the TV screen is sawing a woman in half right before your eyes. What the retailer is doing is juggling prices.
Then I should like to quote from that same article the words of a great supporter of those ideas which most of us think contribute greatly to the general welfare of the people. I refer to Mr. Justice Brandeis.

Perhaps it was, but I prefer to quote part of it in the context of what I have to say. I am not quoting the whole of it, but he says:
Shall we, under the guise of protecting competition, further foster monopoly by creating immunity for the price-cutters?
That, Mr. Speaker, I think is a question that should be answered effectively in the minds of every one of us before we are prepared to support a measure of this kind. We have sought to put before this house arguments that are directly related to this extremely important subject. I submit that no argument that has yet been presented from this side of the house has been directed to anything but the consideration of this subject. It is by all means the small purchaser, dealing with either the small or large store, who must be considered by the members of this

house in passing legislation. Starting from that premise, however, we should not too lightly disturb a long-established commercial system whose whole existence is dependent upon the satisfaction of that small purchaser.
Why are these stores located all over this country today? Why are these small stores spreading into every community, that they have almost become part of the home life of our people? They are there because the people of this country are supporting them. If the people did not believe in the system that has been in practise they had other places to go. They have shown their support of the large store through their mail order business, and when they visited the larger cities. The larger stores had no reason to complain about lack of business, but under this system the small stores have been able to give that kind of service which means so much to all our people. Let us not destroy all the drug stores across this country with the suggestion this is the device by which they make so much money that all they can do is go ahead and put on fancy fronts, gilt and glitter instead of giving efficiency; that is what the minister said. If the members of this house think that, then they put a very low estimate upon the judgment of the people of this country.
Think of what happens in so many cities, towns and villages. The drug store is no further away from the home than the telephone. Most people who have a telephone can call a drug store and have the things they want delivered. They not only get what they want; they get something they know is going to be good. They get something that is produced by a manufacturer whose name has been before them as the manufacturer of quality articles. They know their families are going to be safe when that particular article is used. That is a consideration which should not be overlooked when we have presented to us such strong arguments on behalf of these small stores which are giving service to our people, and which are so much a part of the life of our people that even in difficult days they carried thousands of dollars in debts on their books rather than refuse goods to customers.
These merchants have played their part in the life of this country, and I believe the people of this country know that. I think they want these merchants to be able to continue to give service. Competition has not been disposed of. There is still competition between manufacturers, and there is competition in service between the stores themselves. Surely this government is not putting before us the suggestion that they are turning the clock back more than one hundred years to the one historic doctrine the Whig

party ever had, the old Manchester doctrine of complete and unrestrained freedom of commerce. I cannot believe it. They certainly have never indicated their support of that belief in recent years. It should be remembered that the doctrine which can best be described as that of "the devil take the hindmost" is pure competition. If this argument is being based on pure competition, then I suggest that the history of all the agony that followed the acceptance of that principle be recalled when we are considering something that has to do with the method which recognizes that there has to be some balance between completely unrestrained competition and severely restricted competition.
What we want is competition under the rule of reason. We want competition which is in the interests of the people. It is within the powers of the government to do something about that matter. Other governments have done so. Because their commercial methods are so similar to ours, it is not inappropriate to recall-as has been recalled by other hon. members, including the minister-that forty-five of the forty-eight states in the United States have fair trade laws under which agreements of this kind, where they are not against the public interest, are approved and validated.
In this country an effort was made to introduce an act of that kind. It was a Conservative government that introduced a kind of law which I gather the C.C.F. party now believes in. That was a measure known as the Dominion Trade and Industry Commission Act. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will remember that measure quite well because, as I recall it, he was counsel in the case that followed. I think that is correct, is it not, Mr. Prime Minister?

In other words the court held that this matter did not come within the general trade and commerce provisions of the British North America Act, and that it did not come within the criminal provisions. I suggest that is a consideration that should be dealt with before this high court of parliament deals with this subject. Parliament should be quite sure that a subject which was regarded as being outside the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, where it was to be dealt with in a positive way, is within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada when it is to be dealt with in a negative way.
I think the amendment, now before the house, namely that this bill be not now read but that it be read some day six months hence, could be regarded as something more than merely a blocking motion. I suggest that it could be regarded as a motion which would give the government an opportunity to examine a number of things that have not yet been examined, if the evidence the government has in its possession has really been placed before the house. I express the opinion that there is a grave question as to whether the bill now before us is within the jurisdiction of this parliament. I should like the Minister of Justice to tell the house what independent opinions he has had as to the validity of this measure. I know that practice has been followed generally in the case of similar legislation in the past. Independent counsel of the highest standing have expressed their opinion, and that opinion has been presented to this high court of parliament before parliament was called upon to act.
I believe this measure deserves further consideration. We are putting this motion forward in what we believe to be the best interests of the people of Canada. We regard this measure simply as a red herring to distract attention from the failure of the government to act with regard to inflation. No matter what the purpose may be, however, having regard to the close relationship between the consumers of this country and the small stores I urge the government not to disregard the arguments that have been made, and to take further time to consider so important a step affecting the welfare of so many Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate at this late hour of the session I should like to say first that perhaps I can express an opinion that has not heretofore been voiced, and I want to be very fair in what I say. In the first place, I have had some experience in manufacturing a product which people today cannot buy for five cents, but which is not worth any more than five cents. In the second place, I have had considerable experience in wholesaling, or jobbing as some people call it. By virtue of this experience I did have an interest in the retailer. I will be frank and say my primary interest in him was his ability to pay his bills. I approach this argument from that standpoint on rather short notice, and. also, I must admit, after hearing what I think has been one of the finest debates hon. members have ever listened to in the house, to my knowledge. True, it was heated at times; but none of us can honestly say that we regretted that heat, because it did generate ideas and opinions that to my way of thinking, and I believe to most of us, should be taken into serious consideration.
Let me say first, Mr. Speaker, that I was not a member of the committee that had the privilege, if I may term it such, of reviewing some aspects of the MacQuarrie report. I say now that I have interest in this legislation as a consumer and for other reasons, as I have just stated. I went into the committee room for the purpose of hearing what was going on. Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I regret having to say this, but never before in my experience here-and I can also speak for hon. members who have served in this house much longer than I-was a committee engineered-and I use the term "engineered" advisedly-as this one was. They could have threshed old straw, but they were not even permitted to do that.
I have said to my friends that if I were to make up my own mind on this problem I would want to have an expression of opinion from those much more qualified than I am; and I was not prepared to adopt the ideas expressed by any member of that committee, nor will I be prepared to make up my mind and come to a sane conclusion on the merits of this proposed legislation, in view of my experience, without having before me the evidence of those most concerned. That would include the manufacturer, the jobber, the retailer and the consumer. When I found
TMr. Drew.]

to my amazement, and I think to the amazement of this country, that this committee were in such a terrific hurry that they would not permit representations by the retailers who were so vitally concerned, I wondered, as did these people and those friends of each one of us in this house, what they would think.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the committee room was not big enough to accommodate representation from the ordinary consumer from every province of this country so they could watch what went on in the committee. It certainly would have been an eye-opener to each and every one of them. I hope-and I think I share the opinion of many in this house-that never again will a committee be set up that will be bridled as this one was. It might never have been set up, because it served no purpose except to express to the people of this country the conclusion that this government was determined to go through with the proposed legislation which, they tried to give the impression to the public, was going to benefit them.
That opinion has been shattered so far as the public is concerned, and the opinion of the government has been shattered, as we all know, by the last five by-elections, but the point I make is this. The committee was not permitted to hear evidence which was so vital to everyone. There is no one in this country more entitled to hear what may be said for or against price maintenance than the people vitally concerned. When I see a big company like Eaton's giving their stamp of approval to this type of legislation it makes me wonder-and I represent 45,000 or more people who I think share my convictions-what can be behind it. Mind you, I would not be taking up the time of the house if I thought for one moment that any member of this government had the slightest idea that this legislation would reduce the cost of living. We are all concerned about the cost of living, but I defy any member of the government to stand up tonight or any other time and say that this proposed legislation is going to reduce the cost of living. Not so long ago the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) stood up in this chamber and said- I do not propose to quote his words in detail -that this legislation would have little if any effect on the cost of living. When I see big business stepping into the picture and expressing their well-conceived ideas to the committee I begin to wonder as a common man just what it means.
I should like to give an illustration in order to substantiate what I have been saying. Some people in the house may not

like what I am going to say, and some people in industry may not like it, but 1 do not care. I feel that the moment you take on the responsibility of being a member of the House of Commons you expose yourself to the bar of public opinion and you must be fair to your people regardless of whom you might hurt. That has been my attitude in the past and it will continue to be my attitude as long as 1 am in this house.
I am going to recite to you an experience I had with big business some twenty years ago when I was engaged in the jobbing business, mainly of tobacco. At that time we had at the head of the Imperial Tobacco Company a man who conceived the idea that he was going to have a monopoly in the tobacco business. I want to be fair and say that his successors did not share his views. I know that the present president of the Imperial Tobacco Company certainly does not have the same ideas that man expressed and intended to put into effect. They started a price war because they were the largest unit in the tobacco manufacturing industry in Canada. They also had some jobbing outlets in the various provinces. This particular president had the idea that they were going to get it all. At that time we had a margin of about 11 per cent on gross turnover. Let me be frank and say that was more or less by agreement between the jobbers and manufacturers. In addition to having jobbers in the various provinces this company had the United cigar stores as their retail outlets.
In order to have an almost complete monopoly in Canada they decided to cut prices and put the jobbers out of business. There is no denying that fact. They had practically control of the tobacco industry, and they had control by that time of the cigar manufacturing industry. There is no denying that, and I think some hon. members on the other side will agree. This particular individual decided that he wanted to control the tobacco industry from the production angle, and they decided to cut prices through their jobbers.
Every individual in business is entitled to a fair profit, but no more. I hold no brief for certain retailers who have been getting exorbitant profits. I think there are people in the retail business today who are not good merchandisers. I can say that from experience. Whether the retailers like it or not, I am going to say that there are some retailers in this country who enjoy a higher margin of profit than they should get or could get by with if they were smarter merchandisers.

In order to get control-I think this has to do with the principle of this particular bill -this company decided to give discounts through their wholesale outlets. Then they made the suggestion that they would be interested in buying out other wholesalers who were their competitors. You and I- I am speaking to the members of the house- believe in good sound competition; we do not believe in monopolies or cartels. The point I am trying to make is that if either a government or business pursues a policy whereby any individual or corporation can by means of an act of parliament or legislation of any other sort become a monopoly, or conduct their business in such a manner that there is really no competition, that is not good for any type of business nor is it good ultimately for the consumer. If a large corporation, such as Eaton's, want to get rid of a well-known brand, if they have little industries of their own making that particular product they will undersell the nationally-known brand for no other purpose than to enhance the sale of their own product with the ultimate object of putting out of business the little independent manufacturer producing the goods which were originally sold to all retailers. Let there be no mistake about that.
We must be on our guard today. I appreciate the views that have been expressed by hon. members on the other side, but we must be on our guard against any individual or corporation which is not just looking forward to tomorrow but to fifteen, twenty-five, or fifty years from tomorrow. The basis of our business system today is competition. I think everyone will agree that competition and the product itself are what govern the price.
I have something to say which I am sure will be of interest to hon. members, in view of the fact that the T. Eaton Company made certain representations to the committee on this proposed legislation. I should like to place on the record, though it may have been done before, a statement by Mr. Justice Louis Brandeis, when he said:
The Sherman law seeks to protect men in the right freely to compete, and to prevent practices which must result in compressing competition. It seeks to preserve to the individual both the opportunity and the incentive to create. It seeks to encourage individual effort. The right of an individual manufacturer in a competitive business to market his goods in his own way-by fixing, if he desires, the selling price to the consumer-is in entire harmony' with the underlying principle of the Sherman law.
And it was John Ruskin who said:
It's unwise to pay too much, but it's worse to pay too little.
And the people should remember this:
When you pay too much, you lose a little money -that is all. When you pay too little, you sometimes lose everything, because the thing you bought was incapable of doing the thing it was bought to do. The common law of business balance prohibits paying a little and getting a lot-it can't be done. If you deal with the lowest bidder, it is well to add something for the risk you run. And if you do that, you will have enough to pay for something better.
Few people in Canada know the difference between vertical price cutting by a manufacturer to protect his brand name and goodwill and horizontal price agreements between manufacturers. Mr. Justice Holmes said:

Mr. Speaker, after listening with close attention to the very able address of the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy), I feel that perhaps I can confine my remarks to ten or fifteen minutes.
It was not my privilege to serve as a member of the committee on resale price maintenance, but I did take the opportunity of attending a number of the sittings and listening to the discussions, as I felt this legislation was of great importance. I can assure the house I found them most interesting indeed.
There has been a desire on the part of hon. members who have taken part in the debate to discuss the matter seriously, and I believe that thus far the debate has been conducted along that line. It is true that there have been sharp clashes reflecting different points of view, but that is to be expected when we are dealing with legislation as important as this.
After listening carefully to a number of discussions in the committee on resale price maintenance I must admit I was somewhat puzzled as to the reason for bringing this legislation before the house now, without having further evidence to justify its support. I do feel that had the matter been given greater consideration following the report of the MacQuarrie committee, which I believe was based principally on theory and not on fact, the government would have refrained from taking what I consider such a drastic step. At the beginning everyone realized that this measure was undertaken by the government in good faith. Most of us believed it was an attempt to do something about the high cost of living, but since this debate has started that has been disproved. We can all agree that that is not the case. My opinion, sir, on the basis of the debates in the committee, would be that action against this resale price maintenance structure would not be in the interests of the consumer, as the sponsors of the bill would have us believe. Until more evidence is submitted I could not


possibly support the bill before the house. When a measure as important as this, and of such far-reaching consequences, comes before this House of Commons I feel we should have sufficient time to debate and discuss every detail of it.
We were elected from 262 constituencies across the country for the purpose of giving thorough and earnest consideration to every bill that comes before the house. That is our responsibility. I feel that we would be derelict in our duty as members if we did not study this bill very carefully, despite the fact that it is close to Christmas and many of our members would like to catch a train tonight if they could. I should like to be among them. I do feel sincerely that we have to give careful consideration to this bill, because it has such far-reaching implications. Those who are urging the banning of resale price maintenance describe this measure as one which will protect the consumer from high prices, and which will ensure proper competition. We will all concede those are desirable and admirable objectives. We would all like to see that happen. It has become apparent, however, that this matter of resale price maintenance is not as simple as it seemed in the speech from the throne.
When this legislation was announced, the protests that were registered came chiefly from the small retailer across this country. His contention was that the huge retail organizations would undersell him, and would gradually force him from the sale of those lines of goods. As the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) pointed out the other evening, many of our returned soldiers across this country have set up small businesses, and have become established under the present system. I, for one, could not support legislation that might interfere with the success of those enterprises. I feel that powerful retail establishments would be in a position to dictate prices on their own terms. There is not a member in this House of Commons who would want to see a monopoly in any kind of business. I have sufficient confidence in the members of all parties to believe that is so. But we would not want to see business controlled by large corporations of any kind. We have the Combines Investigation Act on the statute books of our country for the purpose of preventing such an occurrence. I feel that the banning of resale price maintenance could not help the situation, but would create the very condition the government and parliament are attempting to avoid.
Every member of this house knows full well that competition is maintained at the

production level, and that any concern about it at the retail level is not warranted. Prices simply cannot be held at exorbitant levels, except under illegal combine, at the manufacturing end. I believe it is not the retail end of sales about which we should be concerned. It seems significant, Mr. Speaker, and this fact was mentioned by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) this afternoon, that the only group which submitted evidence to the parliamentary committee that was 100 per cent in favour of banning resale price maintenance was the group which comprises the huge organizations, and which is now increasing to the point where its members could be well described as giants in industry. This fact alone would indicate to me, and I take it to many members of this house, that we should not plunge into the banning of resale price maintenance without further study of this tremendously important step.
When the manufacturer sets the retail price of his article he knows he is setting that price in competition with other resale price-maintained goods and he is also setting that price in competition with goods not in that category or classification. As was pointed out in the committee, if the government would concentrate on ensuring the rigid enforcement of the law forbidding combines and cartels it would assure unrestricted competition, and I doubt very much if we would have any reason to fear resale price maintenance in the retail field.
' During these long week ends when we Ontario members occasionally go home on Friday night and come back on Sunday evening, we have the opportunity of consulting with our constituents. During the last three or four week ends I have been conducting a sort of one man Gallup poll amongst the people of my constituency on this very matter. I will say that the people of Haldimand county are intelligent people. They study these matters carefully, and I found them fairly well informed about this legislation and the extent of the discussion that had taken place in this house. They are somewhat concerned about one or two matters in connection with this bill. They are concerned as to what the result will be when price maintenance is removed from price-maintained lines. I also found that they want to be able to buy everything they require at any store in the neighbourhood, particularly the little corner store near their residence; that is one thing which is very important to these people. They like to feel they can buy as cheaply in one store as they can in another, and receive what they consider is honest dollar for dollar value. They also want to retain the privilege
Combines Investigation Act of choosing between branded goods and other goods not price-maintained. I strongly urge the government to hold over this legislation for future consideration and study. I feel that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) is one that we should consider seriously because of the implications which this bill might contain.

Combines Investigation Act
That committee had been appointed over a year ago and nobody had heard a word from them until the Minister of Justice wrote and asked them for an interim report on resale price maintenance. Mind you, I will confess that when this subject was first mentioned it seemed to me to be a very attractive thing. Often I would see in the shops Forsyth shirts at $5, right across the country. I would ask myself: Why should a manufacturer tell a retailer that he has to sell that shirt for $5? Why does he have to put a label on it before he sells it to the retailer? Why does he not let the retailer sell at his own price? I felt I should be able to go from one shop to another until I found the shirt at a lower price, and buy it at that price. But a little reflection and the arguments of hon. members on this side of the house have shown me clearly that that is not the right attitude to take in regard to this matter. There is a community of interest between the manufacturer and the retailer. They are in the same business of selling shirts. The manufacturer makes the shirt and sells it to the retailer. He is anxious to have the retailer sell as many of those shirts as possible. That is only common sense, is it not?
Every manufacturer wants to see his goods have a good showing. He wants to see them in the shop windows and wants to see them becoming popular. So he takes a pride in his product. The retailer is just as anxious as the manufacturer to sell as many shirts as possible. The Minister of Justice brought us a statement from the three states who had not been practising these fair trade laws, and I think the parliamentary assistant did the same thing. They held them up as objects to be admired. Why, do you not believe in democracy, the greatest good for the greatest number? What I mean to do is go back a little way in my own experience. I happen to be familiar with the business of a small confectionery store operated by my mother for some years. Other hon. members may recall some of the matters about which I am going to speak. They will remember the five cent chocolate bar, the five cent bottle of pop, the ten cent package of cigarettes. Sales were made at these prices, not as a result of written agreements but by implied agreement between the manufacturers and the retailers to sell at these prices. When, during the first world war, prices of ingredients that went into chocolate bars went up, the manufacturers started to make the bars smaller so that they could still be sold at five cents. Then I remember particularly in connection with the five cent cigar there was an understanding between the manufacturer and the retailer that it would be sold at these special

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: What is the difference?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: The difference is that one is illegal. Horizontal price fixing is between the manufacturers. We will say that the manufacturers of flour agree between themselves to keep the price at a certain level. This is contrary to the Combines Investigation Act. As the commissioner pointed out, these manufacturers had committed an offence. Because there was a disagreement between the government and the wartime prices and trade board, these men were not prosecuted for a breach of the Combines Investigation Act. I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) understands that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: You fellows remember that.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext:
Unfortunately this report was concealed by the government for over twelve months and it was too late to prosecute the offenders. This report was overlooked by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who is so deeply concerned about the independent retailer today, and especially about that homogeneous person, the consumer. Vertical price fixing, which as I say is quite a legitimate thing, is something which takes place between the manufacturer and the retailer. I submit, and I suggest to the Minister of Justice, that vertical price fixing is a legitimate and a natural development

Combines Investigation Act which has been going on ever since there was any trade. If the government is going to interfere with that, I point out that they are doing something that may have startling effects.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Are you sure?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Yes, I feel sure that it will have serious effects upon our economy. The government intends to prohibit resale price maintenance. It intends to prohibit any arrangement between a manufacturer and a retailer as to the price at which the manufacturer's products shall be sold. This leaves the door open to the loss leader practice. The -loss leader practice is an abuse of trade, and it would have been far better if the Minister of Justice had askqd the MacQuarrie committee to advise the government as to what they should do about this loss leader practice rather than about resale price maintenance.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: What is a loss leader?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: A leader of the opposition.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: How many have they lost?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO FORBID THE FIXING OF SPECIFIC OR MINIMUM RESALE PRICES
speechtext: Now, Mr. Speaker, if resale price maintenance is abolished, as the government intends to do, we shall come back to the question of the Forsyth shirt. Tomorrow or the next day, perhaps in- the January sales that have been mentioned, the big departmental stores will advertise Forsyth shirts which formerly cost $5 for $3.98 or $2.98. All the members of the Liberal party can flock in and get their shirts $1.20 or so cheaper than before. The effect will be that the retailer who was doing a legitimate business will not be able to sell any more shirts of that type. I have only mentioned one article. If the practice is as widespread as the Minister of Justice wishes the house to believe, then that performance could be repeated in all the other different lines, and in all the different commodities in the drug business, as well as the hardware business.

Mr. Speaker, I was reviewing the course of this session and I noticed that on October 9, when we commenced, the speech from the throne mentioned the fact that legislation would be brought down based on this report of the MacQuarrie committee. On October 15 the Prime Minister, in his remarks to the house as reported at page 41 of Hansard, said:
... I can say that as regards immediate additional measures to curb inflation, while others may develop, the only one we are prepared to submit at this time is the one that will arise out of this report of the combines committee with respect to resale prices.
